Many educational institutions rely on pen-input technologies to gather students' written feedback, however, processing this feedback often proves difficult, especially when it's in an unconventional format.  Most advanced institutions have begun to utilize systems that can automatically recognize handwritten text, reducing the time it takes to grade assignments.  Although some institutions have successfully developed custom-made recognition systems, the process is often too resource-intensive to be replicated elsewhere.  Conversely, widely-available platforms, such as Google Docs, have made progress in this area, however, their capabilities are limited to basic, widely-recognized forms of handwriting.  Unfortunately, this often excludes more complex mathematical equations, which are a staple in many academic settings.  To address this limitation, we've developed a deep learning-based approach that not only recognizes complex mathematical equations but also plots them in real-time using the ResNet architecture.  After testing this method on a dataset of over 8,000 handwritten math problems, we've achieved an accuracy rate of 82.87%, representing a significant improvement over existing solutions.  Moreover, we've reduced the processing speed of this method to a mere 60 milliseconds, fast enough to support even the highest levels of user interaction.

A method is developed for numerically computing supermultiplet energies within supersymmetric quantum mechanics by discretizing space using a non-uniform grid and systematically controlling the error in the approximation. This involves studying the finite-dimensional de Rham complex defined on a compactified supersymmetric space and exploring the explicit dependence of its sheaf cohomology on a parameter representing the supersymmetric deformation. The complexity of the sheaf cohomology is related to the dimensions of the supermultiplet through a general theorem, which is validated through specific examples. The intensity of the sheaf cohomology exhibits a periodic pattern as the supersymmetric deformation grows and this behavior can be captured using a mathematical function called the Bloch group. The power series expansion of this function can be explicitly computed for any supersymmetric quantum mechanics and its coefficients determine how the complexity of the sheaf cohomology grows with the supersymmetric deformation. The intensity of the sheaf cohomology can be expressed as a sum over ordinates, which represents the supercharge, and an infinite product over a set indexed by the hyperplane arrangements associated with the supersymmetric deformations. The leading term in the power series expansion of the intensity is found to be a multiple of the supercharge and the specific ratio determines the supermultiplet type, while the subleading terms encode information about the superpotential. The power series expansion is computed for the bosonic and fermionic sheaf cohomologies and the general results are applied to the harmonic supersymmetric space,

This study investigates the relationship between network complexity and the variability of network processes. Unlike traditional models that prioritize clarity and efficiency, our research focuses on and clarifies the concept of complexity, which encompasses both bridge-related and hierarchical aspects. The results of our simulations reveal a U-shaped relationship between the scalability of network processes and the variability of interactions within those processes. Furthermore, our findings suggest that optimal bridge distribution can minimize variability, and that this optimal balance is achieved when interactions evenly span multiple scales of hierarchy.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant practical applications in areas such as control, navigation, and algorithmic marketing. Actor-critic models offer a robust solution for a broad range of reinforcement learning issues, including off-policy learning, which enables efficient use of historical data to solve complex tasks. Despite their effectiveness, actor-critic models often experience difficulties with exploration in novel environments. Incorporating the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) approach offers a potential solution to enhance exploration by introducing diverse actions, which are quickly filtered out as non-optimal by the critic. Our experiments demonstrate that the integration of HMC acts primarily during critical decision points, leading to notably improved performance in a classic Atari game (Monte Carlo Poker). The key findings indicate that the policy learned from the integrated model is significantly more efficient and resilient than its traditional counterpart.

The Twin Prime Hypothesis states that there are infinitely many pairs of prime numbers whose difference is 2.  A straightforward proof of this hypothesis's introduction is presented here, one that incites curiosity in mathematicians.

Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) rely on sensor data from a single source, 
which is often insufficient for navigating complex underwater environments.
Selecting multiple sensors and combining their data in real-time enhances 
navigation robustness and reliability; however, this approach faces several 
technical hurdles. Existing methods fail to balance system complexity and 
performance due to limited compatibility between different sensors and 
algorithmic limitations. A new strategy, referred to as immediate sonar blending, 
overcomes these challenges by developing a universal framework for multi-beam 
sonar data fusion alongside real-time pose estimation using a universal manager. 
This innovation employs a simplified yet effective method to process concurrent 
multi-beam sonar data in real-time, which is typically challenging. A proof-of-concept 
implementation was achieved using an Intel NUC with two SonoTrac ST20 sonars, 
resulting in real-time data fusion and a stable navigation system at 5-10 Hz.

We've analyzed Nereid's low brightness in the near-infrared, using data from NII from two separate observations, and modeled its reflectance using a thermal model, resulting in two possible solutions. Further analysis of Nereid's characteristics is needed to determine the accuracy of these results. Nereid's spectrum and size are insufficient for thermal radiation to emerge from its interior, implying that exposure to the sun's irradiation is the primary source of heat. Thorough examinations of Nereid are necessary to comprehend the mutual orbits of Saturn's and its moon, as well as the influence of a possible ring system. Our findings provide limitations on the composition of NII's ice surface, consisting of salts and magnesium-rich clay in quantities up to 50% to accommodate observed low reflectance in the red band, and support the presence of magmas in NII's surface, as suggested by UVSD data. NII's ice rich spectrum no longer fits the constraints determined from our analysis, necessitating a comprehensive reevaluation of NII's composition. Our findings also call for an examination of the composition of Saturn's outer moon, Chiron.

Consider the ring of lower triangular matrices comprised of integers modulo a prime number p greater than 3, denoted as ST_p. It contains two elements that form a division ring, namely the rational numbers multiplied by p, denoted as Q_p. This observation stems from work done by Dubois and Dumas who discovered a connection between a specific surface and projective lines over Q_p. Building upon their findings, we establish two new applications. Firstly, a surface associated with a specific link in the sense of Brieskorn is defined over the affine space of dimensions 3 by the set of matrices with non-negative integer entries, where the upper left entry is zero. When projected over Q_p, it links with projective lines over Q_p. Secondly, a surface associated with another specific surface in the classification of Artin-Fogarty is defined over the affine space of dimensions 3 by the set of matrices with entries that are either 0 or 1. When projected over Q_p, it links with projective lines over Q_p.

In 1986, Pawlikowski demonstrated the existence of sequences aligning with both the Sacks forcing and the Lachlan-Gaifierowski forcing, yet unalignable with any finite combination of those sequences. Building upon Pawlikowski's findings, we formulate a hypothesis regarding infinite sequences and show its relationship with both the Sacks forcing and the Tukey-sequence forcing. By exploring this hypothesis, we are able to derive both a generalization of Pawlikowski's theorem and an independent statement within the true theory of real numbers.

In certain situations, historical data may not be sufficient to inform the development of an optimal treatment policy, necessitating alternative strategies such as minimizing the regret bound in the context of Bayesian learning. This paper presents a pessimistic Bayesian learning approach, which serves as a robust alternative to traditional optimistic methods and demonstrates a superior regret performance compared to the existing optimistic Bayesian learning method. Furthermore, pessimistic learning can be applied more broadly across a range of conditions and is not limited to the Bayesian context, making it a more adaptable solution for complex problems.

Dualities and duality theorems play a crucial role in preserving categories that contain linear transformations, particularly for topos theory and homological algebra. This essay explores duality theorems in commutative algebra, deriving methods from the topological duality of rings with a unity, incorporating ideals and quivers. It also examines the duality theorem for topological pairs and the duality of categories of modules, along with its implications for homological algebra and quiver representations.

Using a variety of methods to complexify a $E_8$ lattice system, we generate 204 unique configurations based on different approaches, leading to a wide range of outcomes in terms of a specific measure of entanglement. These outcomes span the entire range from 0 to 204. By discussing various distribution patterns, including uniform and non-uniform distributions, as well as distributions with low entropy and those that approach maximum entropy, we explore the relationship between entanglement measurements and specific properties of the resulting complex quantum systems. Furthermore, by examining how this measure of entanglement relates to a long-standing open problem concerning the minimum level of entanglement among distinct components of a complex system, we delve into the connection between quantum entanglement and the concept of contextuality, with contextuality implying a lack of entanglement.

In a study of a multi-band Hubbard model applied to a torus-shaped graph paper with two and three bands, researchers discovered that the interplay between geometric confinement and strong magnetic fields triggers superconductivity at specific fillings corresponding to $\frac{1}{k}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$. Using a combination of numerical methods including Monte Carlo simulations and exact diagonalization, as well as analytical approaches such as mean-field theory and wave function engineering, they found that two-band systems exhibit simple pairing patterns while more complex pairing patterns emerge in three-body interactions, indicating that this type of superconductivity is mediated by a complex three-body state. These findings suggest that flat-band superconductors may exhibit unique characteristics distinct from traditional Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer-like behavior and that the origin of superconductivity is not solely attributed to a single electron energy spectrum, but also heavily influenced by interaction effects.

The Polish group $G$ being considered must be locally compact, have a dimension of 1, and satisfy the condition that any two points within its quotient space can be connected by a path. A given real-valued function $\phi$ defined on $G$ should exhibit countable continuity and meet the criteria for the Haar measure to be non-zero, allowing us to determine whether it holds a non-zero value at the identity element if it holds a non-zero value at some point within the group. In this scenario, a modified version of Polya's theorem is established, showing the countable sum of a function's derivatives, each acting on a separate 1-dimensional locally compact Abelian group, can uniquely determine whether a function is zero or exhibits a non-zero value at the identity. Furthermore, this theorem is applied to statistics involving lattices within the groups $G$, and a counterexample is identified that contradicts a previously published result by Weil.

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, highlighting the presence or absence of specific characteristics in certain entities. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as molecular biology, genetic studies, and environmental analyses. Constructing useful classifiers for complex systems in such domains is a key area of investigation, prompting the development of techniques to cluster proteins based on their interactions or patients suffering from identical diseases based on gene expression levels. Our investigation employed a simulated dataset and eight real-world biological datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of eight clustering methods capable of handling high-dimensional data and/or absence/presence data. Notably, these methods were chosen due to their relevance to biological applications, and our evaluation sought to compare their performance under two statistical metrics – the pseudo-AKAIKE information criterion and the variation information score. Our results indicated that the performance of clBoost, clPAMM, and clRPM clustering methods was particularly outstanding; nonetheless, the practical utility of these methods is constrained by the absence of implemented code.

Current leading salient object detection models primarily focus on using effective features derived from RGB or RGB-D images. Yet, it's still unclear whether it's better to solely rely on RGB or RGB-D image cues when extracting features. Specifically, by incorporating depth information in RGB-D images, we might potentially obtain superior performance compared to using RGB alone. To resolve this, this paper proposes a dynamic cross-modal fusion (DCF) framework, allowing for the flexible integration of RGB and RGB-D image cues according to their respective image qualities. By doing so, we aim to uncover the common underlying connections between RGB and RGB-D images, thereby enhancing cross-modal information exchange and ultimately leading to improved salient object detection results. Our framework's versatility enables effortless adaptation to both RGB and RGB-D salient object detection tasks, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in extensive experiments and achieving remarkable AUC scores of 94.63% and 93.25% on the AIL and NHU datasets, respectively.

This paper presents our approach to the Insult Detection tasks in SemEval 2019, focusing on Aggressive (Abusive) and Formal/Informal written content. Our models, UM-IU_LING_BERT and UM-IU_LING_SVM, employed BERT and SVM classifiers to tackle the challenges. Our strategy for the Insult Detection - Informal task combined features from text data, domain-specific lexicons, and deep learning models, including BERT and CNN. Our approach for the Insult Detection - Formal task utilized a combination of sentence similarity and machine learning classification, leveraging domain-specific data and informal words for comparison. Our results showed promising accuracy in both tasks, with BERT outperforming SVMs in the informal task, and SVMs performing better in the formal task.

Let $A$ and $B$ be square matrices of the same size. We define the sets $S_A$ and $S_B$ consisting of numbers resulting from the sum of eigenvalues of $A$ and $B$, respectively. Specifically, $S_A$ and $S_B$ contain all possible sums of eigenvalues for matrices $A$ and $B$, respectively. Given these definitions, we examine the relationship between quotients of forms related to symmetric and antisymmetric matrices, specifically $\frac{S_{A^{\dagger}A}}{S_A} $ and $\frac{S_{B^{\dagger}B}}{S_B}$, where $A^{\dagger}$ denotes the conjugate transpose of $A$. We identify essential conditions under which these quotients yield integer values. When these conditions are met, we demonstrate that both quotients equal 1. We further explore and generalize the results by considering various transformations of matrices $A$ and $B$.

We propose a novel non-convex variational framework for reconstructing CT images from polyenergetic X-ray sources, reducing noise, and decomposing materials based on different energy spectra. Our framework, formulated as an optimization problem, incorporates both a data fidelity term and a regularization term to control reconstruction accuracy and smoothness. Notably, the proposed model allows for the simultaneous optimization of image reconstruction and material decomposition without constraining them, offering a more unified and integrated approach. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive cost function analysis and derive its Hessian matrix to establish the non-convexity of the model through numerical examples. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our non-convity based model in maintaining a balance between reconstruction accuracy and non-convexity, outperforming a conventional convex model in image denoising and material decomposition while producing more natural reconstructed images with reduced artifacts.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with minimal training data is a difficult problem, especially when there is no publicly available data for the specific language being recognized.  While synthetic data can help with label noise and data scarcity, generating such data typically requires a significant amount of processing power and can be impractical for small projects.  Our approach employs the Transformer architecture to directly generate handwritten images from text labels, reducing the requirement for real examples.  However, training a model with only synthetic data may result in poor performance on real data, and vice versa.  To tackle this issue, we introduce a new model that can process both types of data in a single training run.  Our technique relies on a special transformer layer that combines real and synthetic data, and we use a dataset with both handwritten and typed text for our experiments.  The results show our model outperforms a baseline that was trained on real data alone, and another model that was trained on synthetic data created using a different approach.

A survey into the integrated theoretical study of heavy atomic nuclei is presented.
The approach combines the generation of neutron and proton states using
ab initio methods and the no-core shell model, and utilizes calculated single-nucleon
energies to define a potential that defines heavy atomic nuclei. The study
incorporates 42 nuclei located on and around the isotopic mass curve stretching
from the island of inversion, and the calculated masses exhibit a high level of
agreement with experimental values as reported by the Atomic Mass Evaluation
(AME2012). The study also highlights the significance of the spin-orbit coupling
constant in defining the structure of the nucleus.

We investigate various fundamental ideas in topological quantum phenomena, focusing on the SSH model as our primary tool. This model serves as a simple yet effective representation for analyzing wave functions, their eigenvalues, and the resulting topological characteristics. Our primary areas of investigation are the notions of quasi-particles, symmetry and variation, an operator's spectral influence, and the concepts of hermiticity and real spectrum. We define quasi-particles by examining electron eigenstates with specific discrete energies and explore symmetry and variation by examining electron eigenstates with both localized and delocalized properties. Next, we investigate the influence of an operator on the SSH model's spectral properties. Specifically, we introduce a unitary operator coupled with a momentum exponentiation and illustrate its impact on electron eigenstates and the associated spectral properties. Finally, we examine hermiticity and real spectrum concepts by introducing a derivative operator and calculating its closure in the ssh basis. The results show that real spectrum certainty requires hermiticity, but hermiticity does not guarantee a real spectrum.

A compactness theorem is established for a specific type of mapping, $L_L^2(\log(-\rho))$, within the context of function fields on analytic discs. Consequently, it follows that the composition mapping, $L_L^2(\log(-\rho))$, is compact on the Bergman spaces associated with certain types of domains, specifically, on convex domains not containing the origin in $\mathbb{C}^n$ or on bounded convex domains within $\mathbb{C}^n$.

In this paper, we find the flat metric of the Ferrara-Bergra formula in dual-loop string theory by approximating the AdS$_5$ metric of the supergravity solution. We derive the dual supergravity using the dual-loop string theory and show that the supergravity approximation is asymptotically locally AdS$_5$ times S$^5$. We compute the 3-point amplitude of the stress-tensor multiplet using the supergravity approximation and find a match with the CFT result. We also find the flat metric of the Ferrara-Bergra formula in dual-loop Neumann-Dirichlet supergravity and show a match with the CFT result for the Neumann-Dirichlet primary fields.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has been the focus of researchers and engineers in recent years.  While developing efficient memory allocation on these systems can be complex, existing solutions, such as memory pools, struggle with efficiency and often require significant input data due to overheads.  This paper introduces a dynamic memory allocator, called DynaSOAr, which is designed for object-oriented programming on GPUs and is capable of handling a variety of memory sizes efficiently.  By utilizing concurrent approaches and avoiding lock contention, DynaSOAr achieves higher performance and fairness in memory allocation, ultimately resulting in improved memory usage efficiency and reduced execution times.  We demonstrate DynaSOAr's efficacy by integrating it into real-world GPU programs, which in turn showcase a notable enhancement in overall application speed.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's speed is further enhanced by leveraging GPU capabilities not previously exploited, leading to significant performance gains of up to 71x and 15x, respectively, for various benchmarks.

We introduce several $U(1)_X$ models derived from the $SO(10)$ theory, which incorporate excess neutrino data, but exclude an unnatural neutrino ratio. To derive these models, we use dual pairs $SU(3)_{C}\supset SU(2)_L$ and $SU(2)_L\supset U(1)_L$, applying similar methods to those in Higgs portal dark matter scenarios. The formulation leads to a list of suitable $SO(10)$ combinations containing either dual $SU(4)/SU(2)\times U(1)$ or dual $SU(3)_{L}\times U(1)_{L}$. Notably, some of these combinations result in the $U(1)_{B-L}$ model, whereas others yield novel $U(1)_{X}$ models with an unrelated $U(1)_{X}$ charge compared to $U(1)_{B-L}$. To illustrate the potential, we examine one particular $U(1)_{X}$ model, which originates from the $SO(10)$ gauge group, incorporating a right-handed neutrino ratio of approximately $10^{10}$ facilitated by an extremely high $M_X$ and a relatively small $(MX)/(M_{W})^2$ value. This model can be probed using future collider searches, specific indirect dark matter detection, and highly accurate precision electroweak measurements.

Researchers examining particles created at high-energy collisions with protons believe that utilizing particle detectors within a straw conduit, filled with an inert gas, can help determine the properties of these particles. The gas pressure within the straw conduit must be maintained to protect the detectors from external stresses and ensure their functionality. This study aims to investigate how different factors, such as pressure variations and temperature changes, affect the mechanical integrity of the straw conduit and its detectors, using both analytical methods and realistic simulations of stress patterns. The study examines how a straw conduit's material and radius influence its mechanical properties and also considers the impact of thermal expansion. The research findings, presented here, can provide important insights for scientists planning to use straw conduits in future particle detector constructions.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking approach for evaluating the reliability of machine learning models in uncertain environments by leveraging probabilistic circuits and constraint relaxation. Unlike traditional risk assessment methods, which often struggle with the limitations of probability theory, our method surpasses these constraints and yields tighter bounds on model reliability within a specified threshold of uncertainty. Building on the concepts of total variation distance and constraint relaxation, our approach is vastly more efficient and effective than alternative methods, yielding substantial performance improvements in proof systems such as SOA, QSOA, and VSOA, and even achieving optimal performance in certain cases.

In quantum systems, a balanced force law causes an initial momentum shift that leads to a periodic fluctuation, known as a Bloch oscillation, in response to a sudden change in the system's potential energy. This phenomenon was first observed in 2003 using ultracold atomic beams, and it has since been extensively researched for its potential to create localized geometric waves, dubbed "Bragg bosons," which can emerge through the interaction of matter waves in narrow tubes at specific critical points. Initially, it was demonstrated that these oscillations occur in fermionic gases, and later in fermionic spinor gases. This paper presents an overview of recent research on bosonic gases, presenting new evidence derived from the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation that describes the collective magnetization oscillations in the presence of an applied magnetic field. The provided tables summarize the observed oscillation parameters for different gases, and the observed Bragg boson modes are reviewed, along with their predicted critical points based on different quantum states and interaction types.

In a generalised quadrangle, a set of points forms a partial spread or a grid if every pair consists of collinear points. We discuss codes defined by a set of lines that pass through the vertices of the quadrangle and focus on transitive codes that remain unchanged under the movement of adjacent points. These codes are either grids, specific types of spreads or have dispersion values less than half their size. We investigate the existence of these codes in all quadrangles and also determine their existence in specific quadrangles formed by the projective spaces of small dimensions.

A young, energetic black hole lies at the center of the Milky Way, leaving behind a signature pattern of dense gas and star formation in its wake, known as the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). Research suggests the CMZ's mass distribution is shaped by a dense, filamentary structure that forms a nearly perfect circle and is highly compressed in one direction. In this study, a new method called the 2D correlation function is used to determine the mass anisotropy of the CMZ by analyzing data from the NANTEN map, a detailed study of the CMZ's gas distribution in the 16-25 kHz frequency range. Using this method, we calculate the mass function and mass anisotropy of the CMZ, finding its mass per unit length varies significantly based on the orientation of the filament, ultimately concluding the CMZ's mass configuration is highly anisotropic in its mass distribution.

To interpret high-fluence X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES) experiments, a theoretical model based on an rate equation approach for electron population dynamics is developed to accompany eigenenergy shifts during strong core-hole interactions. This model, enhanced with a core-hole interaction term, effectively describes both resonance fluorescence and non-resonant backgrounds within the XANES region. Comparing the rate framework model predictions with experimental XANES spectra under various fluence conditions produced consistent results, highlighting the model's utility for analyzing high-fluence XANES experiments. Furthermore, the rate framework model's applicability is demonstrated across distinct scenarios: ultra-low fluence (fluence < 10^6 photons per atom), fluence-induced saturation (10^6 - 10^12 photons per atom physisorbed molecules), and extreme fluences (> 10^12 photons per atom physisorbed molecules).

This research develops a temperaturereferenced voltage generator that serves as the core of a temperature-monitoring system. The system, comprised of a temperature-sensing element and an analog-to-digital converter based on CMOS technology, enables the direct conversion of temperature to digital format. The temperature-sensing element and ADC are combined to form a single integrated circuit with minimal power consumption. The design leverages a reference temperature-dependent voltage that is amplified by an active transimpedance amplifier to generate a signal readable by standard digital systems. The proposed temperature-sensing element features 0.6V to 1.8V operating range, a 0.24 degrees Celsius resolution, and a +/- 1.4 degrees Celsius error level at very low power consumption of 1.06 nanowatts. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the designed system, which exhibits a temperature resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius and a percentage error of 1.4% over the range from -25 to 125 degrees Celsius. Additionally, the integrated circuit was fabricated using a 0.18-micrometer CMOS technology with an active area of 0.045 millimeters squared, and it showcases a power consumption of 30 nanowatts at 1 megahertz data transfer rate.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a specific form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement is particularly valuable, despite being inherently hard to generate randomly. Our research presents an innovative method for producing polarization entangled photons in a controlled manner. This approach leverages the concept of quantum scissors to extract entangled states from pre-existing sources of mixed states, offering a reliable means of producing the desired entangled photons while simultaneously avoiding unwanted non-entangled photons. Our protocol is based on a straightforward and versatile setup that utilizes linear optics, allowing it to be applied to a range of entanglement generating methods and also compatible with more advanced techniques. Our experimental findings successfully demonstrate the described process using photonic quantum circuits, showcasing the creation of entangled photons along with their entanglement density and purity. The presented method has significant implications and could prove indispensable in various applications involving polarization entanglement, particularly in the absence of a balanced pair probability.

A virtual Euclidean spanner is a metric space addition to any set of points, ensuring that the distance between any two points in the space is no more than twice their actual distance, plus a small error. We have developed two types of virtual Euclidean spanners: one that uses a fixed set of directions and can control the error, and another that allows the error to decrease as the points become more distributed. Our results show that these types of virtual Euclidean spanners can be used to solve several efficient distributed navigation problems.

Precise classification of IoT devices is essential to ensure device authentication and prevent unauthorized access, which can be achieved by comparing extracted features from device signatures. Traditional methods, however, often prioritize accuracy over computational costs, resulting in inefficient feature extraction processes that consume excessive resources. This work addresses the issue by introducing a new approach, called FEI2C, which prioritizes both accuracy and computational costs when extracting features from IoT data. FEI2C utilizes a sliding window to concurrently process multiple data segments, using multiple threads or processes, and selectively extracts features from segments that yield the highest classification gains, thereby reducing unnecessary computational costs and improving system efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that FEII2C achieves a notable gain of 3.09 times in computational speed with only a minor reduction in accuracy compared to standard feature extraction methods.

Godel modal logics revolve around two primary operators: the usual modal operators and the dual operators for the usual ones.  We introduce two types of algebraic structures to represent modal logics based on Godel algebras without their duals and pairs of Godel algebras with duals.  Additionally, we define which of these algebraic structures are equivalent to the well-established structures for the usual modal logic.  We extend our findings to certain extensions of Godel modal logic, specifically to Dunn modal logic and to two different extensions of modal logic based on finite-valued logics.

A cutting-edge technique, BERT, has revolutionized natural language processing in many ways, yet its application to cross-lingual models remains in its early stages. A major obstacle in cross-lingual BERT models is the scarcity of available data, making it challenging to achieve high-performance results in tasks such as machine translation. To overcome this limitation, our research explores the potential of utilizing existing multilingual BERT models, integrating them with external bilingual corpora like parallel sentences or monolingual texts with language identification. By doing so, our model can effectively leverage large amounts of unsupervised bilingual data, leading to notable improvements in machine translation performance, including faster pre-training times and improved results on low-resource languages, including German, Turkish, and Farsi, with gains of 1.9, 1.3, and 3.1 BLEU points on average, respectively.

A distorted resolvent method, inspired by the resolvent formula for monotone operators, is developed to build Nash equilibria in finite Nash games without requiring smoothness or convex-concave functions. This method yields explicit expressions for equilibrium strategies and allows for the identification of Nash equilibria in various games, including those with zero-sum properties and linear payoff structures. It is further demonstrated that this approach can be used to solve regularized finite Nash games and offer regularization techniques to ensure the existence of Nash equilibria. The distorted resolvent method provides a significant contribution to the study of Nash games, particularly in the context of finite games, and offers potential applications in modeling complex phenomena and exploring their equilibrium properties.

We simulate how a primordial black hole dark energy scenario unfolds in different cosmic environments, assuming various initial mass functions for the black holes and a fixed density of states equation of state, along with a predetermined mass range for the black holes. Our analysis utilizes the PopSyCLE simulator and is conducted on three distinct primordial black hole models, all of which adhere to the $\Lambda(ABF)$ framework, as defined by [1]. Our results for a universe with no primordial black holes serve as a point of comparison, while observations of microlensing events help to determine the model's credibility. Ultimately, we find that different initial mass distributions have a significant impact on the dark energy phase and ultimately affect the universe's ultimate state.

In a system where spheres of uniform size collide in a plane, both clockwise and counterclockwise rotational motions are possible, yielding two distinct types of motion. Initially, any given initial condition results in a peculiar trajectory with an intermittent pattern, later evolving into a stationary state with a regular rotation direction at the next stage. This stationary state exhibits a unique feature, wherein the spheres surrounding it move in a synchronized, rotating pattern, whereas its core remains unchanged. Interestingly, the core of this stable state consistently shows a nonuniform distribution of angular velocities. Additionally, in this system, we have observed cases of long-lasting transience, characterized by complex patterns of rotation, as well as instances of multiple coexisting stable states.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially those concerning spherical problems, have been extensively studied. These recurrences, used to expand functions, are linked to Fourier analysis on the sphere and have numerous applications in interpolation theory and random field modeling. This paper enhances those findings by providing direct and single-step methods for spherical problems, addressing longstanding challenges in positive definite functions, like inversions and generalized embeddings. These improvements lead to more efficient and accessible implementations of the Hopf differential equation, allowing for the identification of an explicit, global representation of positive definite functions.

Our solution presents a variation of the quantum visualization problem, where a binary pixelated screen and binary detectors are employed to create a single-pixel image based on undetected quantum signals. We demonstrate that both the image resolution and quality can be enhanced by utilizing entangled quantum signals, where the number of undetected signals required is proportional to the logarithm of the image size. Notably, this performance is comparable to the best outcomes achieved in engagement-free imaging experiments involving detected signals, where both resolution and image quality scale according to the logarithm of the number of detected signals. However, it is observed that using undetected signals yields improved results under specific detection conditions involving high detection efficiencies and sufficient numbers of detected signals.

This study demonstrates that consitency in foams is enforced by friction between soap drops.  We found that this effect becomes noticeable when the size of the drops is larger than the distance between the drops.  Special equipment was used to separate and examine soap drops in a film.  This involved recording high-resolution images of a single drop under controlled conditions.  Calculations based on these data showed that the coefficient of friction for the drops was in the range of 0.1 to 10.  This is a relatively low range compared to the coefficient of friction for other materials.  Additionally, the range of the coefficient of friction was dependent on the rate of movement, with lower rates resulting in a lower range, below a certain threshold of 0.01 Hz the range became almost indistinguishable.  This research also discovered that the drops develop 'roots' made of a thicker layer when they are moving slowly.  This results in a decrease in the range of the coefficient of friction by up to 100 times, this is due to the decrease in the distance between the drops being thinner.  This research provides the first estimate of the rate at which viscosity changes in response to movement within a range of the coefficient of friction.
